title: Dating and Discernment: Wisdom Before the Covenant
subtitle: Choosing a spouse is among the largest decisions a person ever makes, and the culture has handed us almost no wisdom for it. What Scripture, church history, and honest research say about character over chemistry, courtship and modern dating, and the discernment to marry well or to wait.

parts.title: The Decision You Cannot Run a Test On
parts.body:
You are standing inside the largest decision of your life and no one taught you how to make it. Not really. You learned how to choose a college and a career, how to weigh a job offer and a mortgage, and somehow the one choice that will shape every ordinary day for the next fifty years, the person you wake up next to, the co-parent of your children, the witness to your dying, was left to a feeling. You are supposed to know. You are supposed to fall, and trust the falling, and the culture has handed you almost nothing else.

So you swipe, or you do not swipe and wonder if you should, and either way you are exhausted. The app turns a person into a profile and a profile into a verdict you render in half a second, and you have learned to evaluate human beings the way you evaluate a takeout menu, scanning for the one that looks best tonight. Or you have sworn off all of it and you sit at the edge of every gathering wondering how anyone meets anyone anymore, watching couples form by some magic you cannot reverse-engineer, certain that the door is closing and you are doing it wrong.

And under the mechanics there is a deeper confusion, because you cannot tell what you are even supposed to be looking for. The feeling, the spark, the chemistry, everyone agrees that is the thing, and you have felt it before with people who turned out to be wrong for you in every way that mattered. You have also felt nothing for people who were good and kind and steady, and wondered if the absence of fireworks was a verdict. You do not know how to weigh the flutter in your chest against the slow data of a person's character, and no one has ever told you the flutter is the least reliable instrument you own.

The church, for its part, has often been worse than useless here. It taught a generation a tangle of rules about how far is too far and gave them almost no wisdom about the actual question, how to read a person, how to know one, how to tell the difference between a feeling and a foundation. It handed out a courtship method as though a method could substitute for discernment, and it bred either anxiety or rebellion, sometimes both in the same person. It told you whom not to date and never taught you how to choose.

So let me name the thing plainly. You are facing a covenant decision with the tools of a consumer culture, and the two do not fit. You cannot run a trial on a marriage. You cannot return the person if they disappoint you. You are being asked to make a permanent choice on partial information, which is the very definition of the thing the Bible calls wisdom, and wisdom, not chemistry, is what this decision actually requires. The good news is that wisdom can be learned. The feeling cannot teach you. But you were never meant to be led by the feeling.

parts.title: Why This Choice Carries So Much
parts.body:
Few decisions a person ever makes carry the weight of this one, and pretending otherwise is part of how it goes wrong. The choice of a spouse is not the choice of a companion for an evening. It is the choice of the single most determinative human relationship of your life, the one that will set the temperature of your home, the formation of your children, the trajectory of your finances, and the daily climate of your soul for as long as you both live. Marry wisely and you have given yourself a partner in becoming who God made you to be. Marry foolishly and you have welded yourself to a daily friction that will shape you, too, in the other direction. There is no neutral spouse.

The stakes reach the children who do not yet exist. The person you marry is the person who will help raise your children or fail to, who will model for them what a husband or a wife is, what love looks like under pressure, whether the world is safe. You are not only choosing a partner. You are choosing, in advance and sight unseen, the other half of the parenting your children will receive, and the home they will absorb before they can speak. We choose far more than we know when we choose whom to marry.

The stakes are spiritual in a way the romantic frame never sees. Scripture says a husband and wife become one flesh, a real union of two lives, which means the person you marry will either draw you toward Christ or away from him, day after day, by the simple gravity of shared life. The wrong yoke can slowly cool a faith that once burned. The right one can keep a fire alive through seasons when you could not have kept it yourself. You do not marry a person and keep your discipleship in a separate box. The marriage becomes the soil your faith grows in or struggles in for decades.

And the cost of getting it wrong is among the heaviest a person can carry, which is the whole reason discernment matters so much before the vow. A bad marriage is not a thing you can quietly exit. It divides homes, scars children, drains savings, and reroutes the entire course of a life, and the believer who rushed past the wisdom of choosing well often pays for the rest of their years. This is precisely why the discernment before the covenant is not anxious over-thinking. It is the most loving thing you can do for your future spouse, your future children, and yourself. The wedding industry treats the choosing as the easy part and the wedding as the event. It is exactly backward. The choosing is the thing.

parts.title: What Scripture Actually Says
parts.body:
Scripture does not give you a dating method, and the church that pretended it did added to the word of God. What Scripture gives you is something better and harder, a way of seeing, the wisdom to read a person and a life. Start where the wisdom literature starts. He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the Lord, Proverbs says, and in the same breath the book warns that it is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome spouse. The same Bible that celebrates the gift is unsentimental about the cost of choosing badly, and it treats the choice as a matter for discernment, not for a feeling that overrides discernment.

Proverbs is blunt about the most seductive and least reliable measures. Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain, it says, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised. Read that as the verdict it is. The very qualities the culture tells you to chase, the looks, the charm, the spark, are named by Scripture as deceptive, the surface that says nothing about the substance. What the Bible tells you to look for is the fear of the Lord, the orientation of a person's deepest loves, because that, and not the chemistry, is what you will be living with when the looks have faded and the charm has worn thin and the real person is standing in your kitchen on a bad day.

Go to the one piece of clear apostolic counsel on whom to marry, and notice how narrow it is. Paul tells the widow she is free to marry whomever she wishes, only in the Lord. Only in the Lord. The one non-negotiable Scripture names is shared faith, a spouse who belongs to Christ, and Paul elsewhere warns against being unequally yoked, bound in the deepest union to someone pulling in the opposite spiritual direction. This is not snobbery. It is wisdom about gravity. Two oxen yoked together must pull the same way or the plow goes nowhere and both are wounded, and a marriage where the deepest thing in one person is foreign to the other will strain at exactly the point where it most needs to hold.

Watch how Scripture reads character over chemistry in its own stories. When Abraham's servant goes to find a wife for Isaac, he does not look for the most beautiful woman at the well. He prays for a sign of character, and he finds Rebekah by her generosity, a young woman who offers water not only to a stranger but to all his camels, hard and unglamorous service for someone who could do nothing for her. The text wants you to see that her kindness, displayed when no one important was watching, was the data that mattered. Ruth is praised not for her beauty but because all the town knew her to be a woman of worth, her loyalty and integrity established by a track record anyone could check. Scripture keeps pointing your eye away from the surface toward the substance, toward how a person treats the powerless, keeps their word, and serves when there is nothing in it for them.

And Scripture is honest about desire without making it the captain. The Song of Songs celebrates erotic longing inside the covenant with no embarrassment, so the Bible is not against attraction or the spark. But the Song places that fire inside commitment, and it twice charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before it is ready, a warning against stirring up a passion that the covenant is not yet there to hold. Desire is a good servant and a ruinous master. The wisdom Scripture teaches is not to kill the attraction but to refuse to let it lead, to keep the discernment of character in the driver's seat and the desire in its proper, honored, secondary place. Marry someone you are drawn to, yes. But marry, above all, someone whose character you have watched and whose Lord is your Lord, because the drawing will not survive on its own and the character and the faith will carry you both when it falters.

parts.title: How the Church Has Thought About Choosing
parts.body:
Romantic love as the sole basis for marriage is a recent and largely Western invention, and remembering that is the beginning of wisdom, because it frees us to see that our way of choosing is not the only way and may not be the wisest. For most of human history, across most cultures, marriages were arranged or heavily guided by family and community, and while that system carried real injustices the church rightly came to resist, it also carried a sober assumption we have lost, that the choice of a spouse was too consequential to be left to the feelings of two young people alone. The community had a stake and a say, and the elders who knew both families brought a discernment the infatuated could not.

The church across the centuries did not treat marriage as a private romance but as a covenant formed in the sight of God and the gathered community, which is why it placed the banns, the public announcement of an intended marriage, weeks in advance, inviting anyone who knew a reason it should not proceed to speak. That practice embodied a conviction we have forgotten, that other people can see what the lovers cannot, that the community's eyes are part of how God protects a couple from their own blindness. The medieval and Reformation church alike assumed that wise marriage was a matter of counsel, not just of consent.

The Puritans, so often caricatured as enemies of love, actually held a rich and balanced vision of choosing. They insisted that a couple should genuinely love and like each other, that marrying without affection was foolish and cruel, and at the same time they insisted that the affection must rest on the firmer ground of character and shared faith. They counseled young people to seek the advice of godly parents and pastors, to look hard at a prospective spouse's reputation and conduct, and to test whether the attraction was built on anything that would last. Richard Baxter advised choosing for piety and prudence first, for a suitable temper and a sound character, and letting the love grow in that soil. They refused both the cold pragmatism that ignored the heart and the giddy romanticism that trusted it absolutely.

Then came the long shift, gathering speed through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, in which romantic love climbed onto the throne and became the sole legitimate reason to marry. The novels and later the films taught it, the soulmate who completes you, the destined other half, the feeling that justifies everything. Something true was being recovered, the dignity of love and choice against coerced and loveless matches. But something was also lost, the older wisdom that a feeling is a poor foundation for a permanent covenant, and that the community and the character matter as much as the spark. By the late twentieth century the West had made the most consequential decision of a life depend almost entirely on the least reliable instrument a person owns, the infatuated heart.

The recent evangelical reaction to all this was understandable and largely unwise. Faced with a hookup culture, parts of the church reached for a rigid courtship system, scripting the steps and policing the boundaries, hoping a method could deliver what wisdom alone can give. It often bred fear, formula, and a generation taught more about avoiding sin than about discerning a person. The tradition at its best knew better. It never offered a method. It offered counsel, community, character, and the fear of the Lord, and it trusted the slow, accountable work of discernment over both the cold contract and the runaway feeling.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: A believer can study the research on attraction, mate selection, and lasting marriage the way a farmer reads a weather report, gratefully and critically at once, because all truth is God's truth and the researchers have tracked thousands of relationships from the first date to the divorce or the golden anniversary. What follows takes several bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of how to choose a partner carries a hidden picture of what a person is for.

secular.source: The research on what predicts lasting marriage
secular.author: Ty Tashiro
secular.whatItGetsRight: Tashiro gathered the data on which factors actually predict a stable, satisfying marriage and found that the traits the culture chases, looks and intense early passion, predict almost nothing, while less glamorous traits, agreeableness, emotional stability, and shared values, predict a great deal. He shows that people consistently weigh the wrong variables, choosing for the spark and ignoring the temperament they will actually live with. The science quietly confirms Proverbs.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Tashiro's data echoes Scripture almost word for word, that charm is deceitful and the steady character is what lasts, and a believer can receive it gratefully. But his frame is optimization, choosing the partner most likely to yield personal satisfaction, the self maximizing its own outcome. Scripture reframes the whole project. Marriage is not finally about selecting the partner who will make you happiest but about entering a covenant in which you will be made holy, and the question is not only will this person satisfy me but will we draw each other toward Christ. The research corrects the variables. Only the gospel corrects the goal.

secular.author: Aziz Ansari and Eric Klinenberg
secular.whatItGetsRight: Ansari and Klinenberg documented how dating apps and endless choice have reshaped courtship, and named real costs, the paradox of choice that paralyzes, the way profiles reduce persons to commodities, the exhausting sense that someone better is always one more swipe away. They show that infinite options do not make people happier choosers but more anxious and less committed ones, forever optimizing and never landing.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Their diagnosis of the consumer mindset is sharp and Scripture sharpens it further. The app trains a person to evaluate human beings the way one evaluates products, scanning for the best deal, and Scripture calls a person an image bearer, not a commodity to be compared and discarded. The endless searching for someone better is the restlessness of a heart that has made the spouse into a savior, and no human being can satisfy that hunger. The cure is not a better algorithm but a settled heart, one that can commit because it is not asking a person to be God. The book names the disease. Only the gospel quiets the restlessness underneath it.

secular.source: The research on cohabitation and the slide into marriage
secular.author: Scott Stanley and Galena Rhoades
secular.whatItGetsRight: Stanley and Rhoades documented that many couples slide into cohabitation and then into marriage by inertia rather than by a deliberate decision, and that this sliding is associated with poorer outcomes than couples who decide with intention. They distinguish deciding from sliding and show that the couples who consciously choose, who mark a clear commitment, tend to fare better than those who drift across thresholds without ever choosing.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Their finding that deciding beats sliding maps onto the biblical understanding of covenant exactly, a marriage is meant to be a deliberate, public, witnessed decision and not a drift, a vow and not a gradual habit. Scripture would press further than their data, that the union of bodies was designed to belong inside the covenant and not to precede it as a trial, because the one-flesh bond is not a thing to test but a thing to enter. The researchers see that intentional commitment protects a marriage. Scripture names why, because a covenant is not a sliding accumulation of habit but a chosen, sworn, sheltered thing.

secular.source: The science of attraction and passionate love
secular.author: Helen Fisher
secular.whatItGetsRight: Fisher mapped the neurochemistry of romantic love and showed that the intense early phase of passion is a temporary biochemical state, driven by dopamine and built to fade, distinct from the calmer attachment that can follow. Her research demystifies the spark, revealing the fireworks as a real but time-limited phenomenon that the brain cannot sustain, which is precisely why it makes such a poor foundation for a permanent choice.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Fisher's science is a gift to discernment, confirming from the brain what Scripture says from the heart, that the feeling fades and cannot be the foundation. But her frame reduces love to chemistry, an evolutionary mechanism for pair-bonding and reproduction, with no room for love as a covenant choice that outlives the chemistry. Scripture knows the spark will pass and tells you to build on what remains, the steady choosing to seek another's good that the Bible calls love and that no brain scan can capture. Fisher explains why infatuation cannot last. Scripture supplies the kind of love that can, the deliberate covenant faithfulness the neurochemistry was only ever a rumor of.

secular.source: The research on conflict and communication before marriage
secular.author: John Gottman
secular.whatItGetsRight: Gottman's decades of observing couples revealed that how a pair handles conflict, and specifically whether they fall into criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling, predicts the future of a relationship with striking accuracy, often before the wedding. He shows that watching how someone fights, repairs, and treats you in disagreement is far more informative than watching how they court you in the good moments.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Gottman gives discernment a powerful tool, attend to the conflict and not only the romance, watch how this person handles anger, criticism, and repair, because Scripture too judges a person by their conduct under pressure rather than their charm at peace. But his science maps the behavior and cannot reach the heart producing it. Contempt, Scripture would say, is pride, and the cure is not only a better skill but a humbled heart that has seen its own debt forgiven. The research tells you what to watch for in a prospective spouse. The gospel tells you what actually has to change in them, and in you, for the watching to come out well.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same Bible and the same desire to marry wisely still differ over how a believer should go about the process of choosing, and the disagreement is not careless. It runs to how much structure, accountability, and boundary the path to marriage should carry, set against how much ordinary freedom and getting-to-know-you it should allow. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are guarding something real and both go wrong when pressed alone.

views.view: A more structured, accountable, intentional path
views.body: This view holds that the gravity of the marriage decision and the weakness of the human heart call for real structure around the process of choosing, a path with intention, accountability, and clear boundaries rather than the drift of modern dating. It urges couples to involve their families and church from early on, to define where a relationship is headed before deep emotional and physical bonds form, and to guard physical intimacy carefully so that desire does not override discernment. Advocates point to the wisdom of the older traditions, the banns, the counsel of elders, the assumption that the community sees what the lovers cannot, and they argue that the modern dating culture, with its serial heartbreak and its commodifying of persons, is the predictable fruit of a process with no shape at all. They worry that without structure a couple bonds physically and emotionally faster than they can think, mistakes infatuation for love, and is half-married in heart and body before anyone asked the hard questions. The danger they are guarding against is real, a generation forming and dissolving deep attachments casually, accumulating wounds, and stumbling into or out of marriage on a feeling. They are quick to add that structure is not a guarantee, that a method can become a new legalism, and that the goal is not a rigid script but a wise, accountable, unhurried path that keeps discernment in the driver's seat and lets the community help two people see clearly.

views.view: A freer, relationally honest path of getting to know someone
views.body: This view holds just as firmly that marriage is a covenant to be entered wisely, but it trusts the ordinary, somewhat unscripted work of two people getting to know each other well over time. It worries that heavy structure, rigid timelines, and constant external oversight can short-circuit the very knowing that wise choosing requires, producing couples who followed all the steps and still do not actually know the person they married. Advocates argue that you cannot discern a person's character from a safe and managed distance, that real knowledge comes from time spent, conflict survived, and the unguarded moments a too-controlled process never allows, and that the courtship systems of recent decades often bred fear, formula, and couples who married as near-strangers. They prize honesty and freedom in the getting-to-know-you, within the bounds of holiness, so that two people can see each other clearly before the vow. The danger they are guarding against is also real, a fearful, over-managed approach that mistakes following rules for gaining wisdom, that can rush a couple toward the altar on the momentum of a system before they truly know each other, or that breeds anxiety and rebellion in equal measure. They are quick to add that freedom is not license, that holiness and accountability still matter, and that the goal is not casual drift but the honest, unhurried, real knowing of a person, which is the only thing that finally makes a wise choice possible.

parts.title: What Discernment Forms in You
parts.body:
The work of choosing a spouse wisely forms something in you long before it delivers a spouse, and this is a truth the anxious single, frantic to reach the outcome, almost always misses. God uses the discernment itself, and even the waiting, to shape a person who can love well whether or not the marriage ever comes.

He forms patience, the willingness to wait for clarity rather than to grab at relief. The single believer terrified of being alone will seize the first available person to end the fear, and that seizing is the opposite of discernment. Learning to wait, to let a person's character reveal itself over time, to refuse to force a verdict before the evidence is in, is a deep formation of the soul. It teaches you that you are not in a famine, that your worth does not hang on a wedding, and that a covenant decision is worth making slowly. The person who can wait well for a spouse has already become someone better able to keep one.

He forms the capacity to see a person rather than a projection. The infatuated heart does not see the actual human being. It sees a screen onto which it projects its longings, a fantasy wearing the other person's face, and half the heartbreak in the world comes from marrying the projection and waking up to the person. Discernment is the slow discipline of clearing the projection away, of asking what is actually true about this person rather than what you need to be true, of watching how they treat the powerless and keep their word and handle anger. That clear-eyed seeing is a kind of love in itself, and it forms a person who can keep seeing their spouse honestly for the rest of a marriage.

He forms the humility to seek and receive counsel, which the runaway heart despises. Wisdom in Scripture is communal, and the believer who insists on choosing a spouse in private, deaf to the concerns of the people who love them, is not being brave but proud. Learning to ask wise people what they see, and to actually listen when they name something you did not want to hear, breaks the self-sufficiency that wrecks so many marriages before they begin. The one who can be told the truth before the wedding is far likelier to be teachable inside it.

And he forms a settled identity in Christ that does not depend on the outcome. This is the deepest formation of all, and it can only be learned by the single who refuses to make a spouse into a savior. The believer who knows they are already fully loved, already complete in Christ, already a member of his family, can approach the whole question of marriage from rest rather than from panic. They can pursue a spouse without worshiping one, choose without grasping, and even accept a no or a long wait without their world collapsing, because their life was never riding on it. That settled heart is the single best preparation for marriage there is, and it is also, not by accident, the thing that makes a person able to live a full life if marriage never comes.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: Wisdom in choosing is not admired into existence. It is practiced, in concrete acts of attention, counsel, and self-examination, before any covenant is made. None of what follows is a formula, and a formula was never the point. All of it assumes that this decision deserves more discernment than the culture brings to it, and that the discernment can be learned. One word first. You are not running out of time, and a wise wait is far better than a foolish marriage. Better to be single and whole than yoked and at war.

steps: Name honestly what you have actually been weighing in the people you are drawn to. If it is mostly looks, chemistry, and how they make you feel, hold that list next to Proverbs, charm is deceitful and beauty is vain, and ask what you have been missing.

Make a different list, the one Scripture would have you keep. Character, the fear of the Lord, how they treat the powerless, whether they keep their word, how they handle anger. Begin watching for the substance and not only the surface.

If you are in a relationship, ask yourself the one non-negotiable question plainly. Is this person in the Lord, walking with Christ in a way that will pull the same direction as your own faith, or are you considering an unequal yoke.

Slow down any momentum that is outrunning your discernment. If you are bonding physically or emotionally faster than you are actually coming to know the person, name it, and put the knowing back ahead of the feeling.

Invite real counsel. Tell two or three wise believers who know you well about the person or the situation, and ask them honestly what they see, then actually listen, especially to what you do not want to hear. The community sees what the lovers cannot.

Watch the person under pressure, not only at their best. How do they handle conflict, criticism, disappointment, and the people who can do nothing for them. Gottman and Scripture agree that this is the truer data than how they court you.

Examine your own heart for the fear that distorts discernment. Are you considering this person because they are good and right for you, or because you are terrified of being alone. Bring the fear to God before you bring it to a relationship.

If you are unmarried and want to be married, take honest, unhurried steps toward meeting people in good contexts, the church, shared life, friends, rather than either swearing it all off or surrendering to the exhausting churn of the apps.

Do the slow work of actually knowing the person rather than the projection. Spend time across enough settings and seasons to see who they really are, with their family, under stress, when nothing is going their way, and let the real person come into focus.

Have the hard conversations before the covenant, not after. Money, children, faith, family, expectations, past wounds. The couple who can talk honestly about the difficult things before marriage is far better prepared for the difficult things inside it.

Guard the body so the desire does not seize the wheel from the discernment. Scripture honors attraction and refuses to let it lead, and keeping physical intimacy inside its proper place keeps your judgment clear when you most need it.

Be willing to end it if the discernment says no. Ending a relationship that should not become a marriage is not a failure but an act of wisdom and love, for them and for you, and far cheaper now than after the vow.

Build the settled identity in Christ that lets you choose from rest rather than panic, so that whether marriage comes soon, late, or not at all, your worth and your wholeness are not riding on it. This is the deepest preparation for marrying well.

If you marry, marry deliberately and publicly, deciding rather than sliding, entering a witnessed covenant before God and a community, and not drifting across thresholds by inertia. The research and Scripture agree that the chosen covenant fares better than the accumulated habit.

Whether you are choosing or have chosen, become a person of counsel for younger believers facing this decision, offering the wisdom the culture withholds, character over chemistry, faith as the non-negotiable, the community's eyes over the infatuated heart.

Hold the whole question with open hands, refusing to make a spouse into a savior. Pursue marriage wisely if you desire it, receive singleness fully if it remains, and rest in the truth that your life was never riding on the wedding, because it was always held in Christ.
